hints.junior: A payment retry with 100% coverage and a fully green suite still double-charged a customer — coverage never asked whether the retry was actually safe to fire twice.
hints.mid: 'Called twice' is a true statement about a mock — it says nothing about whether a second real charge was the correct outcome, which is the actual risk this code manages.
hints.staff: This isn't even a missed branch — the catch block ran during the test. The mock's scenario just didn't match the production scenario, and no coverage percentage can tell those two apart.

hints.junior: Both modes show the same green test suite result up top — click 'Simulate lost response' to see what actually happens to the charge underneath it.
hints.mid: Retry-without-idempotency-key creates a second real charge when the first response is merely delayed, not failed — the coverage number never moves between modes.
hints.staff: The coverage stays identical between modes on purpose — the number usually cited as 'well tested' doesn't change at all between the safe version and the one that silently double-charges.

hints.junior: Coverage tells you which lines ran, never whether the test checked anything correct about what should have happened — a weak assertion can hit 100% and catch nothing.
hints.mid: Mutation testing deliberately injects small bugs and reruns your suite — if every test still passes, that mutant 'survived,' meaning your suite would let that exact bug ship regardless of its coverage number.
hints.staff: Mutation testing doesn't fully solve this either — a mutant survives if no test's mock represents the risky real-world scenario in the first place. The reliable complement is naming the worst realistic failure and confirming a test targets it directly.

hints.junior: Zero coverage on a file is a real signal — nobody's looked at it. 100% coverage isn't the mirror-image good signal it looks like; it just means every line ran once, under some test.
hints.mid: Stryker Mutator runs against your existing suite and reports a mutation score alongside your coverage number — 100% line coverage with a 40% mutation score is an honest red flag either number alone would miss.
hints.staff: When full mutation testing isn't practical, add a risk-review question to code review itself: for money, auth, or data-integrity code, name the worst realistic failure and require a test asserting against exactly that scenario.

sections.junior: Today's case is about line coverage versus risk coverage — a payment retry function that hit 100% coverage with a fully green test suite, and still double-charged a real customer in production.
sections.mid: Line coverage answers one question — did this line execute — not whether the test asserted anything true about what should have happened.
sections.staff: This isn't even a missed branch — the catch block did run during the test. The mock's scenario just doesn't match the production scenario that actually occurred, and no coverage percentage can tell those two apart.

sections.junior: Coverage only tells you which lines ran, not whether the test checked anything true about the result. Mutation testing asks a better question: if this code were deliberately broken, would any test actually notice?
sections.mid: Mutation testing introduces small, deliberate bugs into your code and reruns the suite against each one — if every test still passes, that bug would ship undetected regardless of what the coverage number said.
sections.staff: Mutation testing has real cost and doesn't fully solve this either — it only catches faults in code your tests exercise with realistic inputs. The reliable complement is a risk-weighted review naming the worst realistic failure the code enables.

sections.junior: Both versions show the same green coverage report at the top. Try simulating a lost response and watch what actually happens to the charge underneath it.
sections.mid: The version without an idempotency key creates a second real charge when the first response is merely delayed, not failed — the coverage number never moves in either version.
sections.staff: This is deliberately not a coverage-number toggle — the number that usually gets cited as well-tested doesn't change at all between the safe version and the one that silently double-charges.

sections.junior: 100% coverage means every line ran, not that anything was verified correctly. Pair it with mutation testing or a deliberate risk review for anything touching money or data integrity.
sections.mid: Mutation testing asks a different question than coverage — if this code were deliberately broken, would any test notice?
sections.staff: Pair mutation testing where practical with a risk-weighted review question for any code touching money, auth, or data integrity.
